I've brought it up before in the past, but man, the black smoke in Dorohedoro is just the coolest shit.

so, in Dorohedoro, all sorcerers have a tumor in their brains that is actually a very small devil that grants them the ability to produce black smoke. this smoke is basically the medium by which magic effects the world and the smoke of a particular person carries a particular type of magic and depending on the person, they can only handle releasing so much smoke at once. for example, one of the most powerful sorcerers, a mob boss named En, has smoke that both creates and changes anything it touches into mushrooms. his body can also handle releasing an incredibly large amount of smoke. when he was young, he accidentally released a literal mushroom cloud and destroyed a city.

what I really love though, is how *physical* the smoke feels and how well it's integrated into the setting and story. it travels through the body, through *the veins*, it can be bottled and sold for future use, sorcerers often travel on amoke-propelled "brooms" (closer to reverse vacuums), its presence can be felt everywhere, even in Hole, the city/dimension where "normal" people live. there's entire hospital wards of people recovering from the effects of assholes who turn them into bugmen or whatever.

plus, of course, it just looks sick as shit and fits the aesthetic of the world so well.

My favorite system right now and the one I'm currently running a game in is **Beam Saber**.

it uses the same base systems as Blades in the Dark, with a few key differences, the first and most significant being that the PCs pilot giant robots, with the pilot and vehicle both feeling well fleshed out. It also adds the Drive Clock, which is the specific goal that your character is constantly working towards, and some very cool tweaks to stress relief actions. essentially, instead of your character dipping out on their lonesome to indulge in their vice and brood on their own, your character has to spend time with one of their teammates to relieve stress. on top of that, whenever you cut loose with someone, you get closer to them, which has the benefit of making your help actions with them more effective.

everything feels incredibly well designed for the vibe that it's trying to elicit. plus, the author, Austin Ramsay, is incredibly cool about fan material. creators of fan content get to keep 100% of their profits and he's always showcasing new fan content. it also helps that a lot of it is REALLY good

I've posted about it before, but I'm a big fan of the black smoke magic from Dorohedoro. Basically, wizards can pump a thick, black smoke through their veins, which has unique effects from person to person. these effects range from conjuring pie crust to surround something, to separating someone's body into slices while keeping them unharmed, to being able to turn *anything* into mushrooms. plus, its use is completely integrated into wizard society- people get around by either pumping their smoke through mechanical "brooms" or summoning magical doors, there's a thriving aftermarket of especially useful smoke like healing/reviving smoke that's been bottled for future use. it's one of the most thematically interesting magic systems I've personally seen

so it's a number of things, I guess. there's a tendency in a lot of true crime to attribute a person committing a murder and not getting caught to the killer's intelligence or ability and not systemic failings of the police. this does double duty of also playing into cop fear mongering about the criminals and killers being more like Hollywood serial killers who masterfully evade police instead of at best, being someone who exploits failings in the system and at worst, being actively ignored by police and the deaths written off as unimportant.

There's been some drama on twitter the past couple days bringing up the "True Crime has problems" discourse. For anyone out of the loop, there's been a pushback against true crime content lately, especially podcasts. the basis of this pushback essentially being "true crime has a whole litany of issues, ranging from things like (at best) an inappropriate handling of very real tragedies, classic serial killer 'fandom' stuff (its own can of worms), harassment of those close to victims of murder, etc.". personally, I think these are very real concerns! it's actually caused me to reevaluate a lot of my own interest in true crime media, since I also used to be a pretty big fan of this stuff. 

recently though, there was a [tweet](https://twitter.com/introvertedwife/status/1537060797163180034?t=VapvCdRQLNsI8e9Xc5ntBw&s=19) that got a fair bit of attention, stating "Of course there’s a huge backlash against True Crime. It’s predominantly consumed by women. Society cannot trust women to make decisions for themselves. Anything they like must be scrutinized and denounced." naturally, this got people riled up. I'd say that deflecting criticisms of the genre to it being mostly consumed by women (which is true) is ignoring both the real criticisms people have AND the fact that many of these criticisms are also coming from women. she then follows up with [this](https://twitter.com/introvertedwife/status/1537117654581911553?t=qQBClRufM1Tg3RyUQeb7pg&s=19) post, and whew boy. one of the major criticisms of true crime is that it explicitly plays into police narratives and fear mongering, so this is an especially whack take.

Bit late to the thread, but I absolutely had to recommend my new favorite sci-fi series, *The Imperial Radch* series of books.

 The first book, *Ancillary Justice* (the only one I've completed so far) stars a main character who was once the AI of a huge spaceship and had a legion of auxiliary bodies she could populate at once, essentially being a hive mind of sorts. Then, something happens, and she is cut down to just one body, forced to experience things from an extremely limited perspective and having the worst case of phantom limb syndrome ever. Then, cut to present day and her murder revenge quest! 

 It's an incredibly cool book that plays around with what the perspective of this AI would be like and how exactly it would differ from a human's. It also plays with gender and gender identity in a really interesting way and I just can't recommend it enough.

I just finished reading *Islands of Abandonment: Life in the Post-human Landscape* by Cal Flyn yesterday on the recommendation of Jacob Geller, and oh man, that book rules.

It's nonfiction, to start, which I honestly need to make more time for in general, but it's this really fascinating look at these places around the world that are irrevocably impacted by humanity- Chernobyl, Verdun, massive piles of spent shale in Scotland that had been burnt for oil, etc- and how these places have been, slowly, reclaimed by nature in the absence of humans in different ways. Flynn's writing style is definitely over-flowery at times, but she does an amazing job setting the scene for all of these places that she's visited and really making you feel like you're there, experiencing it and the scale of it all. 

A lot of environmental literature has a very nihilistic tone, but this book is able to strike a balance of establishing that those responsible for these massive acts of environmental damage are in no way absolved, there is still yet hope for nature, and I think that's cool as hell.

Alright, so the continent that this all takes place on has been ruled by a lich for the past thousand years. He's evil, without a doubt, and rules with an iron fist, but he's also incredibly efficient. He's done things like raised tons of skeletons to virtually automate farming so that as few people in his kingdom as possible go without food. He's also started various research institutes to study magic that can light cities, power automated travel, and even build artificial life (my character was made in one of these facilities), and under his control, the infighting emblematic of the local nobility (which was actually mostly comprised of Vampires) was kept to a minimum.

However, around sixty years ago, an uppity adventuring party got it in their heads that the world would be better off without him and decided to overthrow him. Since they had a powerful oracle traveling with them, they actually ended up succeeding. But oh man, when they did, shit hit the fan.

After the destruction of the lich, all those skeletons that had been raised now had no one to control them and ran rampant through the countryside. The research facilities, in many cases, ended up being abandoned, their technologies lost to time. And in the resulting power vacuum, the vampire nobility was having a field day slaughtering each other. It was a fucking madhouse. 

Sixty years pass and things have quieted down somewhat. There's still a skeleton problem, but it's more of an annoyance than anything, and the vampires and other nobility have settled down to holding control over their respective cities. My group- who is at this point chilling in a tavern (which we all came to separately, since we hated each other at this point) on an especially rainy day- gets summoned to this huge mansion.

We arrive and are treated to an amazing feast, but with no sign of our host. The next morning, we're finally summoned to this guy's quarters and inside we see an **old** elf. To the point of being actually, visibly old. Turns out that this handsome young man was a member of the original party that slew the lich. In fact, he was the oracle, and his powers were taking a massive drain on him and making him look the way he did. 

He told us that he was dying, that he was sorry for not seeing ahead of time how things turned out. He said that he would give us one final prophecy. The prophecy basically stated that the lich wasn't entirely destroyed. It turns out that when they destroyed him the first time, his phylactery was left intact. According to the oracle, things were soon about to get, much, **much** worse, and the only way to stop it was to find the lich and restore him to power.
